30-60-90 DAY PLAN

Earn trust.
Understand the business.
Then shape the team.

Listening, relationship building, and team assessment run in parallel. The goal is an informed direction and shared commitment before major structural changes.

UNDERSTAND THE PROBLEMS. EARN THE RIGHT TO CHANGE THEM.

Learn fast.
Build trust. Plant seeds.

The need for change is clear. The right fixes will take more than an outside diagnosis. I would get into the conversations where decisions are made and work gets done, learn as much as I can as quickly as possible, and understand why the current structure operates the way it does before changing it.

  • Spend time with leadership, regional teams, recruiters, agents, team leaders, and brokers. Ask direct questions, observe the work, and connect what people say with what the data shows.
  • Build trust by listening closely, following through, and recognizing what already works. Understand where regional independence adds value and where it creates friction.
  • Plant seeds of change through those conversations: shared goals, clearer accountability, national coordination, and equal attention to recruiting and retention. Give people a role in shaping the direction.
  • Build relationships with key producers while assessing the team’s capability, attitude, and willingness to adapt. Reconnect with my network to develop a future talent bench.

Outcome: A clear view of what needs fixing, trust with the people who will make it happen, and the beginnings of shared commitment to change.

NEMAWASHI: LAY THE GROUNDWORK FOR CHANGE

Find the champions.
Build the conviction.

Nemawashi (根回し) is an informal Japanese business practice of laying the groundwork, gathering feedback, and building consensus before making a formal proposal or announcement. This would be my philosophy: involve people early, pressure-test the direction together, and build support before asking the organization to change.

  • Find my “champions of change”: credible leaders and team members who see the opportunity, are willing to adapt, and can help bring others along across regions.
  • Start gaining buy-in around the growth vision and proposed changes through direct conversations. Listen to objections, incorporate useful feedback, and connect the national strategy to each team’s priorities.
  • Assess capability, results, coachability, and attitude. Identify who can lead the next chapter, who needs development, and where the organization needs new talent.
  • Reach out to my network of prospecting, recruiting, and strategic sales talent. Begin conversations about the vision and build a bench of people who could strengthen the team as the structure takes shape.
  • Align leadership and key stakeholders on recruiting quality, retention, shared standards, and the changes with the greatest impact on net agent growth.

Outcome: Champions of change across the business, meaningful buy-in for the growth vision, and a developing talent bench to support it.

DESIGN A PATH PEOPLE CAN EXECUTE

Recommend the structure.
Prepare the transition.

Bring leadership an evidence-based recommendation for roles, management, regional coordination, and talent. Confirm what should change, what should stay, and how to sequence the work.

  • Evaluate the three-role national model against what I have learned.
  • Define responsibilities, progression milestones, and coaching expectations.
  • Prepare a phased implementation and talent plan, including the existing team and my network.

Outcome: An agreed direction and a practical roadmap for the next phase.
